lessons.title: Calculate CPU execution time
lessons.summary: Combine completed instruction count, cycles per instruction and clock period in one fixed-frequency measurement.
lessons.body:
Two processors can run at the same clock frequency and complete the same task in different times. Clock speed alone does not specify how much useful work a processor completes.

To reason about CPU performance you need one equation. Computer architects call it the **iron law of processor performance**, and every other lesson in this module is about improving one of its three terms.

## The equation

For one thread’s measured CPU execution interval at a fixed clock frequency, using matching instruction and cycle counts, run time is the product of three ratios: instructions per program, cycles per instruction and seconds per cycle.

```formula
T = IC × CPI × T_clk
T_clk = 1 / f
T = (IC × CPI) / f
where
T: the CPU execution time of the measured interval, in seconds (s)
IC: instruction count: how many instructions actually executed and completed in the interval, not how many lines the program has
CPI: cycles per instruction: the total counted clock cycles divided by IC, so an average over the whole run; it can be below 1 on a core that finishes several instructions per cycle
T_clk: the clock period, the length of one clock cycle, in seconds; a fraction of a nanosecond on a modern CPU
f: the clock frequency, how many clock cycles happen per second, in hertz (Hz); for example 3 GHz, which is 3 × 10^9 cycles per second
In words: run time is how many instructions you execute, times how many clock cycles each takes on average, times how long one cycle lasts.
```

What each term really means:

- **IC** (instruction count) is the dynamic count of architecturally completed instructions in the measured scope, not how many lines it has. A loop of 3 instructions that runs a million times contributes 3 million.
- **CPI** (cycles per instruction) is total counted cycles divided by completed instructions. It is not the average latency of individual overlapping instructions.
- The **clock period** is the length of one cycle, the reciprocal of the clock frequency.

The clock period follows directly from the frequency. For a 3 GHz clock:

```formula
T_clk = 1 / f
T_clk = 1 / (3 × 10^9 Hz)
T_clk ≈ 0.333 × 10^-9 s = 0.333 ns
where
T_clk: the clock period, the length of one clock cycle, in seconds (s)
f: the clock frequency, here 3 gigahertz (GHz), which is 3 × 10^9 hertz
Hz: hertz, one cycle per second
s: seconds
ns: nanoseconds; 1 ns = 10^-9 s, a billionth of a second
≈: approximately equal to (the result is rounded)
In words: at 3 GHz a single clock tick lasts about a third of a nanosecond.
```

With variable frequency, use compatible cycle/time accounting or sum over fixed-frequency intervals. Waiting off-CPU and concurrent threads need separate accounting; CPU time is not automatically wall-clock response time.

The units cancel neatly: instructions × cycles per instruction × seconds per cycle leaves seconds. That is a good check whenever you do one of these calculations.

### A first calculation

A program executes 2 × 10⁹ instructions with an average CPI of 1.5 on a 3 GHz CPU. First count the cycles, then divide by how many cycles happen each second:

```formula
N_cyc = IC × CPI
N_cyc = 2 × 10^9 × 1.5 = 3 × 10^9
T = N_cyc / f
T = 3 × 10^9 / (3 × 10^9 Hz) = 1 s
where
N_cyc: the total number of clock cycles the program takes
IC: instruction count, the number of instructions executed; 2 × 10^9 here
CPI: cycles per instruction, the average clock cycles per instruction; 1.5 here
T: the run time, in seconds (s)
f: the clock frequency, 3 GHz = 3 × 10^9 cycles per second
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
s: seconds
In words: 2 billion instructions at 1.5 cycles each is 3 billion cycles, and a 3 GHz clock gets through 3 billion cycles in exactly one second.
```

## Key takeaways
- Use matching instruction, cycle and time scopes at a fixed clock frequency.
- CPI is a measured average; overlapping instruction latency is a different quantity.
- Account separately for off-CPU waiting and variable frequency.

## Further reading
- [MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining](https://computationstructures.org/notes/performance/notes.html)
- [Linux perf tutorial](https://perfwiki.github.io/main/tutorial/)

- [MIT: processor-performance equation and pipeline mechanics](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/c15/c15s1/)

This multiplies by the frequency (4 × 10⁹ × 0.8 × 2) instead of dividing by it. Time is cycles divided by cycles per second.
This divides by CPI as if it were IPC. A CPI of 0.8 means fewer cycles than instructions, so the cycle count is 3.2 × 10⁹, not 5 × 10⁹.
This ignores CPI entirely and assumes one cycle per instruction.

lessons.title: IPC and the three performance knobs
lessons.summary: Read IPC and understand how algorithms, compilers, instruction sets and circuits affect the performance equation.
lessons.body:
The previous unit combined instruction count, CPI and clock frequency to obtain CPU execution time. This unit reads the same counts as IPC and asks which design decisions change them. All comparisons still need matching measurement scopes.

## IPC: the same idea, inverted

Modern processors can finish several instructions in one cycle, which makes CPI less than 1. People then usually quote its reciprocal, **IPC** (instructions per cycle):

```formula
IPC = 1 / CPI
T = IC / (IPC × f)
where
IPC: instructions per cycle: completed instructions divided by counted cycles; above 1 when a core finishes several instructions per cycle on average
CPI: cycles per instruction, the reciprocal of IPC
T: the CPU execution time, in seconds (s)
IC: instruction count, the number of instructions executed
f: the clock frequency, in hertz (Hz): cycles per second
In words: IPC is CPI turned upside down, so a higher IPC means less time for the same instructions at the same clock.
```

A CPI of 0.5 is an IPC of 2. Both describe the same measured instruction/cycle totals; IPC is just more natural when the number is above 1. Linux's `perf stat` can report IPC when compatible counters are available and permitted. This is an illustrative, trimmed transcript, not a measurement performed for this lesson:

```
$ perf stat ./myprog
  3,000,000,000  cycles
  6,000,000,000  instructions
    # 2.00 insn per cycle
```

(Actual tool output and available events depend on the system.) Here 6,000,000,000 instructions divided by 3,000,000,000 cycles gives the 2.00 shown, which is a CPI of 0.5.

## Who controls which term?

The three terms are not independent knobs. Each is influenced by different people, and improving one often hurts another.

| Term | Mainly set by | Example |
|---|---|---|
| IC | Algorithm, compiler, ISA | Different sorting algorithms |
| CPI | Microarchitecture, compiler | Pipelining, caches |
| Clock period | Circuit design, process | Logic depth, voltage |

- **The algorithm** can substantially change the work required. Hardware instructions, accelerators and compiler transformations can also reduce architectural IC. The best improvement depends on the measured bottleneck.
- **The compiler** changes IC (removing redundant work, vectorising four additions into one instruction) and CPI (ordering instructions so they don't wait on each other).
- **The instruction set** (ISA) matters too. x86's `rep movsb` encodes a repeated byte copy using one instruction encoding. Implementation work and performance-event counting of repeated instructions need inspection; one compact encoding is not a count of the operations performed. Instruction count is not a fair standalone comparison across ISAs; counts also depend on vectorization and other instructions.
- **The microarchitecture** (how the chip implements the ISA) drives CPI: pipelining, branch prediction, out-of-order execution and caches all aim to lower it.
- **The circuit and process technology** set how short a cycle can be.

## Key takeaways
- IPC and CPI are reciprocals for the same counted instructions and cycles.
- Instruction count is dynamic, so source lines and executable size do not determine it.
- Changing an algorithm, compiler or implementation can affect more than one performance term.

## Further reading
- [Linux perf tutorial](https://perfwiki.github.io/main/tutorial/)
- [MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining](https://computationstructures.org/notes/performance/notes.html)
- [RISC-V unprivileged ISA specification](https://riscv.github.io/riscv-isa-manual/snapshot/spec/)

- [MIT: processor-performance equation and pipeline mechanics](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/c15/c15s1/)

questions.prompt: `perf stat` reports **2.5 insn per cycle** for a run. What is the average CPI?

options.explanation: That is the IPC itself. CPI is its reciprocal.
1 divided by 2.5 is 0.4. A value of 0.25 would correspond to IPC 4.
Correct. CPI is the reciprocal of IPC: 1 / 2.5 = 0.4 cycles per instruction.
CPI of 1 would mean one instruction per cycle. An IPC above 1 means the core is finishing more than one instruction per counted cycle on average, so CPI is below 1.

questions.workedExample:
IPC and CPI are the same ratio of matching counter totals, turned upside down:

```formula
IPC = N_inst / N_cyc
CPI = N_cyc / N_inst = 1 / IPC
CPI = 1 / 2.5 = 0.4
where
IPC: instructions per cycle, the figure `perf stat` reports; 2.5 here
CPI: cycles per instruction, the average clock cycles per completed instruction
N_inst: the number of completed instructions counted
N_cyc: the number of clock cycles counted over the same interval
In words: 2.5 instructions per cycle is the same as 0.4 cycles per instruction.
```

This describes more than one completed instruction per counted cycle on average, without implying each instruction has latency below one cycle.

questions.prompt: For sufficiently large inputs, suppose a replacement sorting algorithm performs substantially fewer operations and hence fewer executed instructions. Which iron-law term is directly reduced?

options.text: The clock period
options.explanation: Clock period is not the term directly reduced by this change. Actual frequency can still respond to software-selected policies, load, temperature and hardware control.

options.text: CPI
options.explanation: Changing the algorithm may also change CPI substantially through locality, branches and dependencies, but fewer executed instructions directly reduces IC.

options.text: Instruction count
options.explanation: Correct by the premise. Big-O operation counts alone do not specify the exact machine-instruction count or the input-size crossover.

options.text: None; algorithms only affect memory use
options.explanation: Algorithms affect both work and memory behaviour. Abstract operation counts and dynamic machine instructions are related, but not identical.

questions.workedExample:
IC counts dynamically executed instructions. Reducing that count directly changes IC, while CPI and actual clock may also change.

To see why a better algorithm can cut work so much, compare the operation counts of an O(n²) and an O(n log n) sort, where n is the number of items, at a million items:

```formula
n^2 = (10^6)^2 = 10^12
n × log_2(n) ≈ 10^6 × 19.9
n × log_2(n) ≈ 2 × 10^7
where
n: the number of items to sort, 10^6 (one million) here
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n: the power you raise 2 to in order to get n; log_2(10^6) is about 19.9
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: at a million items, n squared is a million million while n log n is only about twenty million.
```

Their ratio is not a measured speedup: constants, cases and operation costs matter.

lessons.title: Compute CPI from an instruction mix
lessons.summary: Use a hypothetical additive cost model to find which instruction class contributes most to average CPI.
lessons.body:
A program mixes arithmetic, memory and control-flow instructions. This unit uses an explicitly additive teaching model: the listed cycle costs do not overlap. Real superscalar measurements need consistent cycle attribution rather than the sum of instruction latencies.

## CPI is an average over an instruction mix

For a simple non-overlapping cost model, assign a cycle cost to each instruction class. The overall CPI is then its instruction-frequency-weighted average. On an overlapping superscalar processor, adding individual instruction latencies would double-count shared cycles; a measured CPI breakdown needs a consistent attribution method. The following numbers are hypothetical additive costs:

```formula
CPI = Σ_i (F_i × CPI_i)
where
Σ_i: sigma: add up the bracketed term over every instruction class i
i: one instruction class, such as ALU operations, loads, stores or branches
F_i: the fraction of executed instructions that belong to class i, between 0 and 1; all the fractions add up to 1
CPI_i: the cycle cost of one instruction in class i, in clock cycles
CPI: the average cycles per instruction over the whole mix
In words: the overall CPI is each class's cycle cost weighted by how often that class occurs.
```

Here is the calculation in Python for a hypothetical mix:

```python
mix = {          # fraction, cycles
    "alu":    (0.50, 1),
    "load":   (0.20, 5),
    "store":  (0.10, 3),
    "branch": (0.20, 2),
}
# Weight each class by its frequency.
cpi = sum(f * c for f, c in mix.values())
# Output: average cycles per instruction.
print(round(cpi, 2))   # 2.2
```

The same working by hand:

```formula
CPI = F_ALU × 1 + F_load × 5
      + F_st × 3 + F_br × 2
CPI = 0.5 × 1 + 0.2 × 5 + 0.1 × 3 + 0.2 × 2
CPI = 0.5 + 1.0 + 0.3 + 0.4 = 2.2
where
CPI: the average cycles per instruction over the mix
F_ALU: the fraction of instructions that are ALU (arithmetic and logic) operations, 0.5 here, each costing 1 cycle
F_load: the fraction that are loads, 0.2 here, each costing 5 cycles
F_st: the fraction that are stores, 0.1 here, each costing 3 cycles
F_br: the fraction that are branches, 0.2 here, each costing 2 cycles
In words: weighting each class's cycle cost by its share of the instructions gives an average of 2.2 cycles per instruction.
```

Notice that loads are only 20% of instructions but contribute 1.0 of the 2.2 cycles, almost half. This is how architects decide what to optimise: find the term that dominates the weighted sum. Halving the load cost (5 cycles to 2.5) saves 0.2 × 2.5 = 0.5 cycles per instruction and brings CPI to 1.7; halving the ALU cost (1 cycle to 0.5) saves only 0.25 and brings it to 1.95.

## Key takeaways
- Weight each class cost by its share of executed instructions.
- Do not add overlapping instruction latencies as if execution were serial.
- Compare weighted savings before choosing which class to optimise.

## Further reading
- [MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining](https://computationstructures.org/notes/performance/notes.html)

- [MIT: processor-performance equation and pipeline mechanics](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/c15/c15s1/)

questions.prompt:
In an additive class-cost model with non-overlapping cycle costs, the instruction mix is as follows. What is its average CPI?

| Class | Fraction | CPI |
|---|---|---|
| ALU | 40% | 1 |
| Load | 30% | 4 |
| Store | 10% | 2 |
| Branch | 20% | 3 |

options.explanation: This is the unweighted mean of the four CPIs, (1 + 4 + 2 + 3) / 4. Each class must be weighted by how often it occurs.
That is the worst-case class CPI (loads), not the average.
This is only the loads' contribution (0.3 × 4). The other classes add another 1.2.

questions.workedExample:
Weighted average: multiply each fraction by its CPI and add.

```formula
CPI = Σ_i (F_i × CPI_i)
CPI = 0.4 × 1 + 0.3 × 4
      + 0.1 × 2 + 0.2 × 3
CPI = 0.4 + 1.2 + 0.2 + 0.6 = 2.4
where
CPI: the average cycles per instruction over the whole mix
Σ_i: sigma: add up the bracketed term over every instruction class i
i: one instruction class: ALU, load, store or branch
F_i: the fraction of instructions in class i: 0.4, 0.3, 0.1 and 0.2
CPI_i: the cycles one instruction of class i costs: 1, 4, 2 and 3
In words: weighting each class's cost by how often it occurs gives 2.4 cycles per instruction on average.
```

Loads are 30% of instructions but half of all cycles (1.2 of 2.4).

questions.prompt: Using the mix from the previous question (ALU 40% at 1, load 30% at 4, store 10% at 2, branch 20% at 3), which single improvement gives the biggest speedup? Keep instruction count and clock fixed, and assume additive independent cost reductions.

options.text: Make ALU instructions take 0 cycles
options.explanation: Even removing ALU cost entirely only saves 0.4 cycles per instruction: CPI 2.0, a 1.2× speedup.

options.text: Halve the branch CPI from 3 to 1.5
options.explanation: Saves 0.2 × 1.5 = 0.3: CPI 2.1, about 1.14× faster.

options.text: Halve the load CPI from 4 to 2
options.explanation: Correct. Saves 0.3 × 2 = 0.6: CPI 1.8, a speedup of 2.4 / 1.8 ≈ 1.33×.

options.text: Halve the store CPI from 2 to 1
options.explanation: Saves only 0.1 × 1 = 0.1: CPI 2.3, about 1.04× faster.

questions.workedExample:
Compute the cycles saved per instruction (fraction × CPI reduction) for each option:

```formula
R_i = F_i × d_i
R_ALU = 0.4 × 1 = 0.4
R_br = 0.2 × 1.5 = 0.3
R_ld = 0.3 × 2 = 0.6
R_st = 0.1 × 1 = 0.1
S = 2.4 / (2.4 − 0.6) = 2.4 / 1.8 ≈ 1.33
where
R_i: the cycles per instruction saved by improving class i
F_i: the fraction of instructions in class i
d_i: the reduction in that class's cycle cost: ALU 1 → 0, branch 3 → 1.5, load 4 → 2, store 2 → 1
R_ALU, R_br, R_ld, R_st: the saving for ALU, branch, load and store improvements
S: the speedup from the best option, old CPI divided by new CPI, with instruction count and clock fixed
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: halving the load cost saves the most, 0.6 cycles per instruction, taking CPI from 2.4 to 1.8, about 1.33 times faster.
```

Rule for these options: compare fraction × achievable CPI reduction. The largest original cycle share wins only when the feasible fractional reductions are equal; engineering cost matters too.

lessons.title: Compare machines and compiler changes
lessons.summary: Calculate total time or cycles when clock rate, instruction count and CPI change together.
lessons.body:
Use the fixed-frequency iron law from the earlier units. Each example below changes one or more terms, so a headline clock rate or instruction count cannot settle the comparison.

## Comparing machines correctly

The iron law stops you being fooled by any one number.

### Faster clock, slower machine

Same program, same instruction count (10⁹). Machine A runs at 2 GHz with CPI 1.2; machine B runs at 3 GHz with CPI 2.0. Apply the iron law to each:

```formula
T_A = (IC × CPI_A) / f_A
T_A = 10^9 × 1.2 / (2 × 10^9 Hz) = 0.60 s
T_B = (IC × CPI_B) / f_B
T_B = 10^9 × 2.0 / (3 × 10^9 Hz) ≈ 0.67 s
where
T_A, T_B: the run times on machines A and B, in seconds (s)
IC: instruction count, 10^9 instructions on both machines
CPI_A, CPI_B: the average cycles per instruction on each machine: 1.2 and 2.0
f_A, f_B: the clock frequencies: 2 GHz (2 × 10^9 Hz) and 3 GHz (3 × 10^9 Hz)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
s: seconds
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: B's clock is faster, but it needs so many more cycles per instruction that it still finishes later.
```

A is about 1.11× faster despite a clock 33% slower.

### More instructions, less time

The same trap catches compilers. Compiler X emits 1.0 × 10⁹ instructions at CPI 1.1; compiler Y emits 0.8 × 10⁹ instructions at CPI 1.5. On the same clock, compare total cycles:

```formula
N_X = IC_X × CPI_X = 1.0 × 10^9 × 1.1
N_X = 1.1 × 10^9
N_Y = IC_Y × CPI_Y = 0.8 × 10^9 × 1.5
N_Y = 1.2 × 10^9
where
N_X, N_Y: the total clock cycles for the code from compilers X and Y
IC_X, IC_Y: the instruction counts: 1.0 × 10^9 and 0.8 × 10^9
CPI_X, CPI_Y: the average cycles per instruction: 1.1 and 1.5
In words: X runs 25% more instructions but needs fewer cycles in total, so on the same clock X finishes first.
```

When you compare, compute **total cycles** (IC × CPI) on the same clock, or total time on different clocks. Never compare one term in isolation.

### Speedup

Performance is the reciprocal of time, so "A is S times faster than B" means:

```formula
S = T_B / T_A
S = 0.667 s / (0.600 s) ≈ 1.11
where
S: the speedup of A over B: how many times faster A is; above 1 means A is faster
T_A: the run time on machine A, in seconds (s); 0.600 s in the first example
T_B: the run time on machine B, in seconds; 0.667 s in the first example
s: seconds
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: speedup is the old (or other) time divided by the new time, so a bigger number means a bigger win.
```

Be careful with phrases like "50% faster": it means a speedup of 1.5, not that time fell by 50% (which would be a speedup of 2, twice as fast).

## Key takeaways
- On one fixed clock, compare total cycles; on different clocks, compare execution time.
- A reduction in instruction count can lose if CPI rises enough.
- Speedup divides old time by new time; halving time doubles speed.

## Further reading
- [MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining](https://computationstructures.org/notes/performance/notes.html)

- [MIT: processor-performance equation and pipeline mechanics](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/c15/c15s1/)

questions.prompt: Both machines execute the same workload, and each retires 10⁹ instructions. Machine A: 2.5 GHz, CPI 1.0. Machine B: 4 GHz, CPI 1.8. Which is faster, and by how much?

options.text: B, by 1.6×, because its clock is 1.6× faster
options.explanation: This compares only clock rates and ignores that B needs 80% more cycles per instruction.

options.text: A, by 1.8×, because its CPI is 1.8× lower
options.explanation: This compares only CPI and ignores that B's cycles are shorter.

options.text: They are equal
options.explanation: Only true if CPI divided by clock frequency were the same for both. A spends 0.4 ns per instruction; B spends 0.45 ns per instruction. These follow by dividing each CPI by the corresponding clock frequency.

options.text: A, by about 1.125×
options.explanation: Correct. A takes 0.4 s; B takes 0.45 s. 0.45 / 0.4 = 1.125.

questions.workedExample:
Time per instruction is CPI divided by the clock frequency:

```formula
t = CPI / f
t_A = 1.0 / (2.5 GHz) = 0.400 ns
t_B = 1.8 / (4.0 GHz) = 0.450 ns
T_A = 10^9 × 0.400 ns = 0.40 s
T_B = 10^9 × 0.450 ns = 0.45 s
S = T_B / T_A = 0.45 / 0.40 = 1.125
where
t, t_A, t_B: the average time per instruction (on machine A or B), in nanoseconds (ns)
CPI: cycles per instruction: 1.0 on A, 1.8 on B
f: the clock frequency: 2.5 GHz on A, 4.0 GHz on B
GHz: gigahertz, 10^9 cycles per second; dividing cycles by GHz gives nanoseconds
ns: nanoseconds, 10^-9 seconds
T_A, T_B: the total run time of the 10^9 instructions, in seconds (s)
S: the speedup of A over B
s: seconds
In words: A spends 0.40 ns per instruction and B 0.45 ns, so A is 1.125 times as fast.
```

In this model, B’s higher clock does not compensate for its higher CPI.

questions.prompt: A program runs 10⁹ instructions at CPI 1.2. A new compiler flag unrolls loops, cutting the instruction count by 20%, but the larger code causes more instruction-cache misses and CPI rises to 1.4. Same clock. What is the speedup?

options.text: About 1.07×
options.explanation: Correct. Old: 1.2 × 10⁹ cycles. New: 0.8 × 10⁹ instructions × 1.4 = 1.12 × 10⁹ cycles. 1.2 / 1.12 ≈ 1.07.

options.text: 1.25×, from the 20% fewer instructions
options.explanation: This assumes CPI is unchanged. The worse CPI eats much of the gain.

options.text: About 0.86×, a slowdown
options.explanation: This compares only CPI (1.2 / 1.4) and ignores the reduced instruction count.

options.text: Exactly 1.0×; the effects cancel
options.explanation: They would only cancel if 0.8 × 1.4 equalled 1.2. It is 1.12, so there is still a small gain.

questions.workedExample:
With the same clock, compare total cycles before and after:

```formula
N = IC × CPI
N_old = 1.0 × 10^9 × 1.2 = 1.20 × 10^9
N_new = 0.8 × 10^9 × 1.4 = 1.12 × 10^9
S = N_old / N_new = 1.20 / 1.12 ≈ 1.07
where
N, N_old, N_new: total clock cycles (before and after the flag)
IC: instruction count: 1.0 × 10^9 before, 20% fewer (0.8 × 10^9) after
CPI: cycles per instruction: 1.2 before, 1.4 after
S: the speedup, old time divided by new time; on the same clock this equals the ratio of cycles
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: 20% fewer instructions at a 17% higher CPI still leaves about 7% fewer cycles.
```

Lesson: code-size optimisations trade IC against CPI. Always measure total cycles; if the larger code causes enough extra instruction-cache misses, unrolling could even be a loss.

```formula

t_old = 1.0 / (3 GHz) ≈ 0.333 ns
t_new = 1.3 / (4 GHz) = 0.325 ns
t_new / t_old = 0.325 / 0.3333 ≈ 0.975
S = 1 / 0.975 ≈ 1.026
where
t, t_old, t_new: the average time per instruction, in nanoseconds (ns)
CPI: cycles per instruction: 1.0 now, 1.3 with the deeper pipeline
f: the clock frequency: 3 GHz now, 4 GHz with the deeper pipeline
GHz: gigahertz, 10^9 cycles per second
ns: nanoseconds, 10^-9 seconds
S: the speedup, old time divided by new time
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the faster clock only just outweighs the higher CPI, saving 2.5% of the time, which is 2.56% higher performance.
```

Power, area and workload measurements are needed to decide whether this hypothetical design trade is worthwhile.

questions.prompt: A job takes 10 s: 3 × 10¹⁰ instructions, CPI 1.0, on a 3 GHz CPU. You need it to take at most 5 s. Which changes, each on their own, achieve that?

options.text: Raise the clock to 6 GHz
options.explanation: In the hypothetical fixed-CPI model, 3 × 10¹⁰ cycles at 6 × 10⁹ per second take 5 seconds. Whether a particular processor can sustain that frequency for this workload is a separate question; 6 GHz is not universally impossible.

options.text: Cut the instruction count to 1.5 × 10¹⁰ at the same CPI
options.explanation: Achieves it: halving IC halves cycles, giving 5 s.

options.text: Lower CPI to 0.6
options.explanation: Not enough: 3 × 10¹⁰ × 0.6 / (3 × 10⁹) = 6 s, a 1.67× speedup.

options.text: Cut instructions by 40% and CPI by 20%
options.explanation: Achieves it: 0.6 × 0.8 = 0.48 of the original cycles, so 4.8 s.

options.text: Raise the clock by 30% and cut CPI by 30%
options.explanation: Not enough: time scales by 0.7 / 1.3 ≈ 0.54, giving about 5.4 s. Improvements multiply; they do not add to 60%.

questions.workedExample:
Time scales by the instruction-count factor times the CPI factor, divided by the clock-rate factor. You need a factor of at most 0.5:

```formula
r = (r_IC × r_CPI) / r_f
r_A = 1 × 1 / 2 = 0.50
r_B = 0.5 × 1 / 1 = 0.50
r_C = 1 × 0.6 / 1 = 0.60
r_D = 0.6 × 0.8 / 1 = 0.48
r_E = 1 × 0.7 / 1.3 ≈ 0.54
where
r: new time divided by old time; it must be ≤ 0.5 to get from 10 s to 5 s or less
r_IC: new instruction count divided by old
r_CPI: new cycles per instruction divided by old
r_f: new clock frequency divided by old
r_A, r_B, r_C, r_D, r_E: the time factor for options A to E
≤: is at most
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: options A, B and D halve the time or better; C and E fall short.
```

Note E: a 30% faster clock and 30% lower CPI do not give 60% less time. The factors multiply.

lessons.title: Avoid misleading performance metrics
lessons.summary: Distinguish task completion time from the MIPS rating, clock frequency and peak throughput scores.
lessons.body:
Earlier units established CPU execution time, IPC and weighted CPI. This unit tests performance headlines against those definitions. The examples remain hypothetical fixed-frequency measurements unless explicitly identified otherwise.

## Misleading metrics

### The megahertz myth

A shorter clock period can be offset by a larger CPI, for example if a deeper design incurs more recovery cycles on mispredicted branches. Exact historical processor stage counts and cross-product performance comparisons are omitted here: they need a specific primary hardware description and benchmark, rather than a general clock-speed anecdote.

### The MIPS rating

The **MIPS rating** (millions of instructions per second; nothing to do with the MIPS instruction set) counts how many millions of instructions a machine completes each second:

```formula
MIPS = IC / (T × 10^6)
MIPS = f / (CPI × 10^6)
where
MIPS: the instruction rate, in millions of instructions per second
IC: instruction count, the number of instructions executed
T: the run time, in seconds
f: the clock frequency, in hertz (Hz): cycles per second
CPI: cycles per instruction, the average clock cycles each instruction takes
10^6: one million, which turns instructions per second into millions of instructions per second
In words: the MIPS rating is the instruction count divided by the time, in millions; equivalently, the clock rate divided by CPI.
```

As a throughput score it does not account for how many instructions the task requires, so it rewards a machine or compiler that runs lots of cheap instructions. For example, on a 1 GHz CPU, compiler P emits 1.2 × 10⁹ instructions at CPI 1.0, and compiler Q emits 0.6 × 10⁹ instructions at CPI 1.5:

```formula
T_P = (1.2 × 10^9 × 1.0) / (10^9 Hz)
T_P = 1.2 s
MIPS_P = (1.2 × 10^9) / (1.2 s × 10^6)
MIPS_P = 1000
T_Q = (0.6 × 10^9 × 1.5) / (10^9 Hz)
T_Q = 0.9 s
MIPS_Q = (0.6 × 10^9) / (0.9 s × 10^6)
MIPS_Q ≈ 667
where
T_P, T_Q: the run times of the code from compilers P and Q, in seconds (s), from instruction count × CPI / clock frequency
MIPS_P, MIPS_Q: each version's score in millions of instructions per second
Hz: hertz, cycles per second; the clock is 1 GHz = 10^9 Hz
s: seconds
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: Q finishes first while scoring a third lower on the MIPS rating, because it simply needs fewer instructions.
```

A MIPS rating can describe instruction throughput, but it predicts task completion time only when the relevant dynamic instruction counts are fixed. The same binary can still execute different counts on different inputs or execution paths.

### Peak numbers

Vendors quote peak IPC or peak FLOPS: what the chip can do if every functional unit is busy every cycle. Real code waits on memory and mispredicted branches. Realized IPC depends on instruction mix, dependency chains, front-end delivery, memory behaviour and prediction. No universal IPC value or dominant bottleneck is asserted for databases or web servers.

> [!tip] Measure, don't guess
> `perf stat` gives you cycles, instructions and IPC for a real run. Low IPC alone does not identify the cause: serial arithmetic dependencies, execution-unit pressure, front-end limits, branch recovery and memory stalls can all contribute. Use architecture-specific counters and profiles before choosing a fix.

## How the performance techniques fit

Every technique in the following lessons attacks one term of the iron law, and usually costs something in another:

- **Pipelining** overlaps instructions so CPI approaches 1 and the clock can be shorter. Cost: hazards.
- **Forwarding and branch prediction** claw back the CPI lost to hazards.
- **Superscalar and out-of-order** execution push CPI below 1 (IPC above 1). Cost: area, power and complexity.
- **Power and thermal limits** constrained frequency scaling and encouraged multicore designs. Frequency did not stop increasing altogether. Multiple cores can improve throughput and can reduce the time of a parallelizable single job.

## Key takeaways
- The MIPS rating measures instruction throughput and predicts time only when the relevant dynamic count is fixed.
- Peak IPC or FLOPS needs a workload and a stated counting convention.
- Low IPC suggests investigation, not a unique bottleneck diagnosis.

## Further reading
- [Linux perf tutorial](https://perfwiki.github.io/main/tutorial/)
- [MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining](https://computationstructures.org/notes/performance/notes.html)
- [Intel: top-down analysis](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/vtune-profiler/cookbook/2024-0/top-down-microarchitecture-analysis-method.html)

- [MIT: processor-performance equation and pipeline mechanics](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/c15/c15s1/)

questions.prompt: Select all statements that are true.

options.text: A compiler that reduces the instruction count always reduces run time
options.explanation: False. Fewer instructions can come with a higher CPI (for example more complex instructions or more cache misses), so total cycles can rise.

options.text: IPC is the reciprocal of CPI
options.explanation: True. IPC is instructions divided by cycles; CPI is cycles divided by instructions.

options.text: For matching CPU-time measurements with fixed dynamic instruction count, a higher MIPS rating means shorter CPU execution time
options.explanation: True: the MIPS rating is the instruction count in millions divided by the run time in seconds, so with a fixed count, a higher MIPS rating means less time. The same executable alone does not guarantee the same dynamic count.

options.text: A higher clock rate guarantees better performance
options.explanation: False. With fixed dynamic instruction count, execution time is proportional to CPI multiplied by the clock period. Compare their product, not percentage changes separately: a 31% CPI rise and a 30% period fall give 1.31 × 0.70 = 0.917 of the original time.

options.text: A program's CPI depends on its instruction mix
options.explanation: True: instruction mix is one influence. Dependencies, cache behaviour and speculation also matter; raw latencies cannot simply be added on overlapping cores.

questions.workedExample:
Lower IC or higher clock alone does not guarantee less time if other terms change. With a fixed instruction count, time is proportional to CPI times the clock period, so the two changes multiply:

```formula
r = (CPI_2 / CPI_1) × (P_2 / P_1)
r = 1.31 × 0.70 ≈ 0.917
where
r: the new run time divided by the old, with instruction count fixed
CPI_1, CPI_2: cycles per instruction before and after; here CPI rises 31%
P_1, P_2: the clock period before and after, in the same time unit; here it falls 30% (a faster clock)
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: a 30% shorter cycle with 31% more cycles per instruction still saves time, but only about 8%, not 30%.
```

IPC and CPI are reciprocal for matching counts. With fixed dynamic IC, a higher MIPS rating implies less measured CPU time. CPI depends on the workload, including mix and interaction between instructions.

questions.prompt:
A single-threaded service runs at a fixed 3 GHz on one core, with matching non-multiplexed instruction/cycle counters for its CPU execution interval. `perf stat` shows:

```
12,000,000,000  cycles
 4,800,000,000  instructions
```

What are the IPC and run time, and what does the IPC suggest?

options.text: IPC 2.5, 1.6 s; the core is running near its limits
options.explanation: This inverts the ratio: 4.8 / 12 is 0.4, not 2.5. The run time is also computed from instructions instead of cycles.

options.text: IPC 0.4, 1.6 s; the code is compute-bound
options.explanation: Time uses counted cycles divided by the fixed frequency. IPC alone cannot determine whether the workload is compute-bound or memory-bound.

options.text: IPC 0.4 and 4 s of counted CPU execution; more evidence is needed to identify the bottleneck
options.explanation: Correct: 4.8 / 12 = 0.4 instructions per cycle, and 12 × 10⁹ cycles at 3 × 10⁹ per second take 4 seconds. Dependencies, execution resources, memory and front-end issues are possible causes; off-CPU waiting would add wall time.

options.text: IPC 2.5, 4 s; the code is well optimised
options.explanation: 2.5 is the CPI, not the IPC.

questions.workedExample:
Divide the counters, then convert cycles to time at the fixed clock:

```formula
IPC = N_inst / N_cyc
IPC = 4.8 × 10^9 / (12 × 10^9) = 0.4
CPI = 1 / IPC = 2.5
T = N_cyc / f
T = 12 × 10^9 / (3 × 10^9 Hz) = 4 s
where
IPC: instructions per cycle
CPI: cycles per instruction, the reciprocal of IPC
N_inst: the instructions counted, 4.8 × 10^9
N_cyc: the cycles counted, 12 × 10^9
T: the CPU execution time of the counted interval, in seconds (s)
f: the fixed clock frequency, 3 GHz = 3 × 10^9 cycles per second
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
s: seconds
In words: the core completes 0.4 instructions per cycle, and 12 billion cycles at 3 GHz is 4 seconds of CPU time.
```

This does not prove that most cycles do no useful work or that memory is the bottleneck. Use suitable profiles and architecture-specific top-down metrics to distinguish causes.

lessons.title: Overlap instructions through five stages
lessons.summary: Trace a load and see why overlapping instructions improves throughput.
lessons.body:
Imagine doing laundry. Each load needs washing (30 minutes), drying (30) and folding (30). Doing four loads one after another takes 6 hours. But the moment the first load moves to the dryer, the washer is free. Start the second load then, and four loads finish in 3 hours.

No individual load got faster: each still takes 90 minutes. What improved is **throughput**, the rate at which loads come out the end. That is pipelining, and it is a fundamental technique in CPU design.

## Executing one instruction

A simplified processor can organize instructions into a common sequence of stages. The classic RISC design, from the MIPS processors of the 1980s and the Patterson and Hennessy textbooks, splits it into five stages:

| Stage | Name | Does |
|---|---|---|
| IF | Fetch | Read instruction at PC |
| ID | Decode | Decode, read registers |
| EX | Execute | ALU op or address |
| MEM | Memory | Load or store data |
| WB | Write back | Write result register |

Follow a load, `lw x1, 8(x2)` (RISC-V: load a 32-bit word using x2 plus an eight-byte offset; on RV64I, sign-extend it into x1):

1. **IF**: read the instruction from the instruction cache at the address in the program counter (PC); compute the sequential next PC by adding four bytes for the uncompressed base instruction used here.
2. **ID**: decode the opcode; read register x2; sign-extend the immediate 8.
3. **EX**: the ALU adds the eight-byte offset to x2 to form the byte address.
4. **MEM**: read the data cache at that address.
5. **WB**: write the loaded value into x1.

Other instructions use a subset. An `add x3, x4, x5` does its addition in EX and has nothing to do in MEM. A store `sw` writes memory in MEM and has nothing to write back. A branch compares registers and decides the next PC.

## With a pipeline

Pipelining puts the next instruction into IF as soon as the current one moves on to ID. Once the pipeline is full, all five stages are busy, each with a different instruction:

```
cycle  1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8
i1     IF  ID  EX  MEM WB
i2         IF  ID  EX  MEM WB
i3             IF  ID  EX  MEM WB
i4                 IF  ID  EX  MEM WB
```

Read it column by column. In cycle 5, i1 is writing back, i2 is in MEM, i3 in EX, i4 in ID, and (if there were one) i5 in IF. From cycle 5 on, **one instruction completes every cycle**: an ideal CPI of 1.

Here is a small Python function that draws the diagram:

```python
STAGES = ["IF", "ID", "EX", "MEM", "WB"]

def diagram(n):
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("bad count")
    k = len(STAGES)
    # First result fills all k stages.
    total = k + n - 1 if n else 0
    for i in range(n):
        row = ["    "] * total
        # Shift this instruction one column.
        for s, name in enumerate(STAGES):
            row[i + s] = f"{name:<4}"
        print(f"i{i + 1:<3}" + "".join(row))
    print("cycles:", total)

# Four overlapping rows; 8 cycles total.
diagram(4)   # ... cycles: 8
```

## Key takeaways
- IF, ID, EX, MEM and WB describe the five-stage teaching pipeline.
- Several instructions occupy different stages simultaneously.
- The ideal scalar pipeline completes one instruction per cycle after filling.

## Further reading
- [MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining](https://computationstructures.org/notes/performance/notes.html)
- [RISC-V unprivileged ISA specification](https://riscv.github.io/riscv-isa-manual/snapshot/spec/)
- [BOOM implementation: pipeline](https://docs.boom-core.org/en/latest/sections/intro-overview/boom-pipeline.html)

questions.prompt: In the classic 5-stage pipeline, during which stage does `lw x1, 8(x2)` calculate the memory address x2 + 8?

options.text: IF
options.explanation: IF only fetches the instruction and increments the PC; it doesn't know yet that this is a load.

options.text: ID
options.explanation: ID reads x2 and sign-extends the 8, but the addition happens in the next stage.

options.text: MEM
options.explanation: MEM uses the address to read the data cache. The address must already exist by then.

options.text: EX
options.explanation: Correct. The ALU in EX adds the base register and offset; MEM then reads memory at that address.

questions.workedExample:
1. IF: fetch `lw` from the instruction cache.
2. ID: decode; read x2; sign-extend the immediate 8.
3. **EX**: ALU computes x2 + 8.
4. MEM: read the data cache at that address.
5. WB: write the loaded word to x1.

questions.prompt: What does pipelining primarily improve?

options.text: The latency of each individual instruction
options.explanation: Each instruction still passes through every stage, and pipeline registers add delay, so the latency of one instruction usually gets slightly worse.

options.text: Throughput: how many instructions complete per unit time
options.explanation: Correct. Overlapping instructions keeps every stage busy, so once full, one instruction completes each (shorter) cycle.

options.text: The number of instructions in the program
options.explanation: Pipelining is a hardware technique; it runs exactly the same instructions.

options.text: Memory capacity
options.explanation: Pipelining is about overlapping execution steps, not storage.

questions.workedExample:
1. Laundry analogy: each load still takes wash + dry + fold.
2. But a new load finishes every 30 minutes instead of every 90.
3. Same in the CPU: a load still visits IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB, but a new instruction completes every cycle.
4. In iron-law terms: CPI approaches 1 and the clock period shrinks to one stage's delay.

questions.prompt: A full 5-stage pipeline has no stalls. Instruction i1 was fetched in cycle 1, i2 in cycle 2, and so on. Which instruction is in the EX stage in cycle 6?

options.text: i6
options.explanation: i6 is just being fetched (IF) in cycle 6.

options.text: i4
options.explanation: Correct. An instruction is in EX two cycles after it is fetched. i4 was fetched in cycle 4, so it is in EX in cycle 6.

options.text: i3
options.explanation: i3 was fetched in cycle 3 and is in EX in cycle 5; by cycle 6 it is in MEM.

options.text: i2
options.explanation: i2 is in WB in cycle 6.

questions.workedExample:
Draw column 6:

```
cycle    1  2  3  4  5  6
i2          IF ID EX ME WB
i3             IF ID EX ME
i4                IF ID EX
i5                   IF ID
i6                      IF
```

With no stalls, instruction j is fetched in cycle j and moves one stage per cycle, so the stage number tells you how far behind the fetch it is:

```formula
j = c − s
j = 6 − 2 = 4
where
j: the number of the instruction (i1, i2, ...) in stage s during cycle c
c: the clock cycle number, counting from 1; 6 here
s: the stage number counting from 0: IF 0, ID 1, EX 2, MEM 3, WB 4; EX is 2
In words: in cycle 6 the EX stage holds the instruction fetched two cycles earlier, i4.
```

lessons.title: Pipeline registers set the clock budget
lessons.summary: Compare a single-cycle clock with the slowest pipelined stage and explain why interstage registers are necessary.
lessons.body:
Continue with the five-stage load/store teaching pipeline: IF fetches, ID decodes and reads registers, EX operates, MEM accesses data, and WB writes a result. The stage delays below are hypothetical. They illustrate timing budgets, not a particular fabricated processor.

## Without a pipeline

A simple **single-cycle** processor does all five steps in one long clock cycle. The cycle must be long enough for the slowest instruction. Using these hypothetical combinational stage delays, with single-cycle boundary overhead ignored:

```
IF   ID   EX   MEM  WB
200  100  200  200  100  (ps)
```

A load uses all five steps, so the single cycle must cover their sum:

```formula
T_1 = t_IF + t_ID + t_EX + t_MEM + t_WB
T_1 = (200 + 100 + 200 + 200 + 100) ps
T_1 = 800 ps
f_1 = 1 / T_1 = 1 / (800 ps)
f_1 = 1.25 GHz
where
T_1: the clock period of the single-cycle design, in picoseconds (ps)
t_IF, t_ID, t_EX, t_MEM, t_WB: the logic delay of each step (fetch, decode, execute, memory, write back), in picoseconds
f_1: the resulting clock frequency, in gigahertz (GHz)
ps: picoseconds; 1 ps = 10^-12 seconds, so 1,000 ps = 1 nanosecond
GHz: gigahertz, 10^9 cycles per second
In words: a single-cycle CPU's clock tick must be as long as all five steps of its slowest instruction put together.
```

So the clock period is 800 ps (1.25 GHz), and each instruction takes one cycle. Most of the hardware sits idle most of the time: while the ALU is working, the fetch unit has nothing to do.

### Pipeline registers

Between each pair of stages sits a **pipeline register** (named IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM and MEM/WB). At every clock edge, each stage's output is latched into the next register. This holds everything the instruction still needs: its operand values, destination register number and control signals (is it a load? does it write a register?). Without these registers, the next instruction would overwrite the values the previous one is still using.

### The clock period

The clock now only needs to cover the slowest **pipeline stage**, not the whole instruction. In reality a pipeline register adds its own delay, setup time and clock skew, which must be budgeted:

```formula
T_clk = t_max + t_reg
t_max = max(t_IF, t_ID, t_EX, t_MEM, t_WB)
where
T_clk: the pipelined clock period, in picoseconds (ps)
t_IF, t_ID, t_EX, t_MEM, t_WB: the logic delay of each of the five stages, in picoseconds
max: the largest of the values listed
t_max: the delay of the slowest stage, in picoseconds
t_reg: the per-cycle overhead of a pipeline register (its own delay, setup time and clock skew), in picoseconds
ps: picoseconds, 10^-12 seconds
In words: every stage gets the same clock tick, so the tick must fit the slowest stage plus the register overhead.
```

Here the slowest stages are IF, EX and MEM at 200 ps. With no overhead the period is 200 ps. Assuming 20 ps of combined per-cycle boundary overhead gives 200 + 20 = 220 ps; this is a teaching assumption, not a measured device value.

## Key takeaways
- The single-cycle period covers the longest whole instruction path in this model.
- The pipeline period covers the slowest stage plus boundary overhead.
- Interstage registers keep one instruction’s operands and controls aligned.

## Further reading
- [MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining](https://computationstructures.org/notes/performance/notes.html)
- [BOOM implementation: pipeline](https://docs.boom-core.org/en/latest/sections/intro-overview/boom-pipeline.html)

questions.prompt: A five-stage pipeline has combinational stage delays of 250, 150, 300, 250 and 100 ps, with 25 ps of per-cycle register overhead. With one cycle per stage and no stalls, how long does one instruction take to pass through the whole pipeline?

options.explanation: That is the single-cycle time. In the pipeline every stage gets a full clock period, whatever its own delay.
This uses 5 × 300 ps and forgets the register overhead.

options.text: 325 ps
options.explanation: That is the clock period, the time between completions, not the time for one instruction to get through.
Correct. The clock is 300 + 25 = 325 ps, so five stages take 1,625 ps, about 55% more latency than the 1,050 ps single-cycle design.

questions.workedExample:
An instruction spends one full clock period in each of the 5 stages, and the period includes the register overhead.

```formula
T_clk = t_max + t_reg
T_clk = 300 ps + 25 ps = 325 ps
L = k × T_clk = 5 × 325 ps = 1625 ps
G = T_1 / T_clk = 1050 ps / (325 ps)
G ≈ 3.2
where
T_clk: the pipelined clock period, in picoseconds (ps)
t_max: the delay of the slowest stage, 300 ps
t_reg: the overhead each pipeline register adds, 25 ps
L: the latency: the time for one instruction to pass through the whole pipeline, in picoseconds
k: the number of stages, 5
G: the long-run throughput gain over the single-cycle design
T_1: the single-cycle period, 1,050 ps, which is also its latency
ps: picoseconds, 10^-12 seconds
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: each instruction now takes 1,625 ps to get through instead of 1,050 ps, yet instructions complete about 3.2 times as often.
```

So latency got worse, while throughput improved.

questions.prompt: A student builds a 5-stage pipeline but omits the ID/EX pipeline register, wiring the decode stage's outputs straight into the ALU. What goes wrong? The rest of the five-stage control and timing is left unchanged.

options.text: Nothing; the register only exists to save power
options.explanation: Pipeline registers are functional, not a power optimisation. They hold the state of each instruction for its stage.

options.text: Fetch becomes slower
options.explanation: Fetch is upstream of ID/EX and is unaffected.

options.text: EX no longer holds the prior instruction’s isolated operand/control state; it instead follows ID, breaking the assumed five-stage sequencing
options.explanation: Correct with unchanged control. Removing the register merges the combinational path; a deliberate four-stage redesign could still work with adjusted timing and control.

options.text: Only branches break
options.explanation: Every instruction passes its operands and control signals through ID/EX, so all of them are affected.

questions.workedExample:
1. In a pipeline, ID and EX hold *different* instructions in the same cycle.
2. The ID/EX register captures, at the clock edge, everything EX needs for its instruction: operand values, immediate, destination register, control bits.
3. Remove it and EX sees whatever ID is currently producing, which belongs to the *next* instruction.
4. The two stages merge into one long combinational path, so you either lose the overlap or get corrupted results.

lessons.title: Fill, latency and pipeline speedup
lessons.summary: Count a finite burst and distinguish instruction latency from long-run throughput.
lessons.body:
Use a scalar five-stage pipeline with one-cycle stages and no hazards. The earlier timing unit used an 800 ps single-cycle period and a 200 ps pipelined period before register overhead; IF, EX and MEM each took 200 ps, while ID and WB took 100 ps. Keep these assumptions explicit in the calculations.

## How much faster?

Take a run of instructions on an initially empty, single-issue pipeline with no stalls. The first instruction needs one cycle per stage to come out, and each later one comes out 1 cycle after the one before:

```formula
N_cyc = k + (n − 1)
where
N_cyc: the total clock cycles from the first fetch to the last write-back
k: the number of pipeline stages; 5 here
n: the number of instructions in the run, at least 1
In words: filling the pipeline costs one cycle per stage, then every further instruction adds just one more cycle.
```

For 1,000 instructions, compare the single-cycle design with the pipelined one:

```formula
T_single = n × T_1 = 1000 × 800 ps = 800 ns
T_pipe = (k + n − 1) × T_clk
T_pipe = 1004 × 200 ps = 200.8 ns
S = T_single / T_pipe
S = 800 ns / (200.8 ns) ≈ 3.98
where
T_single: the total time on the single-cycle design, measured here in picoseconds or nanoseconds
T_pipe: the total time on the pipelined design, measured here in picoseconds or nanoseconds
n: the number of instructions, 1,000
k: the number of pipeline stages, 5
T_1: the single-cycle clock period, 800 ps
T_clk: the pipelined clock period, 200 ps (no register overhead)
S: the speedup: how many times faster the pipeline is
ps: picoseconds, 10^-12 seconds
ns: nanoseconds, 10^-9 seconds; 1 ns = 1,000 ps
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the pipeline runs the 1,000 instructions about 3.98 times faster than the single-cycle design.
```

The ideal long-run speedup approaches the number of stages, here five: that requires perfectly balanced stages, so each stage takes one fifth of the single-cycle period, and no register overhead. We got about 4 for two reasons:

1. **Unbalanced stages.** ID and WB need only 100 ps but get a full 200 ps slot. The pipeline runs at the pace of its slowest stage.
2. **Fill and drain.** The first four cycles have at least one empty stage in this five-stage model. With 1,000 instructions this barely matters (4 cycles); with 5 it would matter a lot.

For a long run, the instruction count is so large that the fill cycles become negligible and the speedup settles at the ratio of the two clock periods:

```formula
S_max = T_1 / T_clk
S_max = 800 ps / (200 ps) = 4
S_max = 800 ps / (220 ps) ≈ 3.6
where
S_max: the long-run speedup as the number of instructions grows very large
T_1: the single-cycle clock period, 800 ps
T_clk: the pipelined clock period: 200 ps without register overhead, 220 ps with 20 ps of overhead
ps: picoseconds, 10^-12 seconds
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: in the long run the pipeline wins by the ratio of the old clock tick to the new one, so register overhead eats directly into the gain.
```

> [!warning] Throughput and latency differ
> With a 200 ps cycle, a single load now takes five cycles of 200 ps, 1,000 ps in all, to pass through, compared with 800 ps unpipelined. In this comparison, pipelining raises throughput while increasing instruction latency. Balanced stages with no register overhead could preserve latency; real overhead and imbalance often increase it. Enough independent work allows the improved throughput to outweigh fill/drain overhead; billions of instructions are not required.

## Key takeaways
- An initially empty unstalled scalar run needs the stage count plus one cycle for each additional instruction.
- Fill/drain overhead matters more for a short burst.
- Stage imbalance and register overhead reduce long-run gains; latency need not improve.

## Further reading
- [MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining](https://computationstructures.org/notes/performance/notes.html)

The latency of a single instruction falls

With perfectly even splitting, each stage gets 1,000 ps divided by the number of stages, plus the fixed register overhead. Latency is one clock period per stage.

```formula
T_clk = 1000 ps / k + 20 ps
L = k × T_clk
k = 5:  T_clk = 220 ps, L = 1100 ps
k = 10: T_clk = 120 ps, L = 1200 ps
k = 20: T_clk = 70 ps,  L = 1400 ps
G_10 = 220 / 120 ≈ 1.83
G_20 = 220 / 70 ≈ 3.14
where
```
