1. Doubling stages gives less than double throughput because the 20 ps overhead does not shrink.
2. Latency grows with every stage added.
3. Not shown here: hazard and recovery penalties depend on the paths being split and can offset clock gains; total stage count alone does not quantify them.

lessons.title: Regular encodings and deeper pipelines
lessons.summary: Explain which ISA properties simplify pipelining and why splitting one stage changes the bottleneck.
lessons.body:
The previous units showed that the slowest stage sets the pipeline period. This unit asks what makes fetching and decoding manageable, and what changes when a designer adds stages. These are implementation choices; the ISA alone does not prescribe one pipeline.

## Why RISC was designed for this

Regular encodings and load/store operations, as in the base RISC teaching model here, simplify pipeline design:

- **Fixed-length base instructions** (32 bits in the model; compressed forms such as RISC-V C differ) let IF fetch one per cycle and let ID start decoding before it knows what the instruction is.
- **Register specifiers** in regular positions across formats, allow register selection alongside opcode decoding.
- **Load/store data operations**: ordinary arithmetic in this model uses registers; separate loads and stores transfer data. Instruction fetch and specialised atomic operations are outside that simplification.
- **Naturally aligned scalar accesses** avoid line splits when their power-of-two size does not exceed the line size and divides it. Real ISAs can also allow unaligned accesses, with additional handling.

x86, with variable-length instructions from 1 to 15 bytes and memory operands on arithmetic, needs additional instruction-boundary and operand handling relative to this simplified fixed-width, load/store teaching design. Many Intel and AMD implementations translate x86 instructions into simple, RISC-like **micro-operations** (µops), and pipeline those.

## Real pipelines

The five-stage design is a teaching model. Real implementations divide work differently, and “pipeline depth” may refer to different instruction paths or recovery events. A cross-product table of stage counts is omitted because comparable primary documentation was not established for every entry.

Splitting a critical stage can shorten the clock period, while adding register overhead and potentially delaying particular result or branch-resolution paths. Not every hazard penalty necessarily increases: that depends on where stages are added and which bypass paths exist.

## Where it goes wrong

The ideal "one instruction per cycle" assumes every instruction can enter the pipeline the cycle after the previous one. Three things break that:

- **Structural hazards**: two instructions need the same hardware in the same cycle.
- **Data hazards**: an instruction needs a result the previous one hasn't produced yet.
- **Control hazards**: after a branch, the CPU doesn't know which instruction to fetch next.

The following hazard units cover each kind and the tricks, chiefly **forwarding**, that keep this pipeline flowing.

## Key takeaways
- Regular register fields and load/store data operations simplify the teaching pipeline.
- RISC-V compressed instructions and real unaligned accesses need extra handling.
- Splitting one stage helps only until another path or overhead sets the period.

## Further reading
- [RISC-V unprivileged ISA specification](https://riscv.github.io/riscv-isa-manual/snapshot/spec/)
- [MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining](https://computationstructures.org/notes/performance/notes.html)
- [BOOM implementation: pipeline](https://docs.boom-core.org/en/latest/sections/intro-overview/boom-pipeline.html)

- [Intel implementation and optimisation manuals](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/intel64-and-ia32-architectures-optimization.html)

questions.prompt: In the simplified base-ISA teaching model, which features make pipelining easier? Here memory access means ordinary data operations, excluding instruction fetch and specialised atomic operations. Select all that apply.

options.text: All instructions are the same length
options.explanation: Correct. The fetch stage can grab one instruction per cycle and know where the next begins without decoding.

options.text: Arithmetic instructions can take operands directly from memory
options.explanation: Incorrect. Memory operands on ALU instructions need a memory access before the ALU, breaking the simple IF-ID-EX-MEM-WB order. This is part of why x86 cores convert to µops.

options.text: Only loads and stores access memory
options.explanation: Correct. A load/store architecture keeps memory access in one stage (MEM).

options.text: Register fields sit in the same bit positions in every format
options.explanation: Correct. Registers can be read in ID in parallel with decoding the opcode.

options.text: Instructions range from 1 to 15 bytes
options.explanation: Variable length adds boundary-detection work. Extra stages or predecoding are possible implementation choices, not a mandatory fixed structure.

questions.workedExample:
Ask, for each feature: does it let each stage do a fixed, simple job every cycle?

1. Fixed length: fetch is trivial. **Yes.**
2. Memory operands on arithmetic: needs memory then ALU then maybe memory again. **No.**
3. Load/store only: memory work stays in MEM. **Yes.**
4. Fixed register fields: read registers while decoding. **Yes.**
5. Variable length: additional instruction-boundary detection is needed. **No.**

questions.prompt: Using stage delays IF 250, ID 150, EX 300, MEM 250, WB 100 ps (no overhead), a designer splits EX into two 150 ps stages, making a 6-stage pipeline. What is the new clock period, and what now limits it?

options.text: 150 ps, limited by the new EX halves
options.explanation: The clock must fit the slowest stage. IF and MEM are still 250 ps.

options.text: 300 ps; splitting a stage doesn't change the clock
options.explanation: It does: the 300 ps stage no longer exists. Only stage delays determine the period.

options.text: 175 ps, the new average stage time
options.explanation: 1,050 / 6 = 175 ps is the average. The clock is set by the maximum, not the average.

options.text: 250 ps, now limited by IF and MEM
options.explanation: Correct. The slowest stage drops from 300 to 250 ps, giving 1.2× more throughput. Further clock gains require shortening the IF and MEM critical paths, for example by splitting them or changing their logic.

questions.workedExample:
The clock must fit the slowest of the new stages.

```formula
T_clk = max(250,150,150,150,250,100) ps
T_clk = 250 ps
G = 300 ps / (250 ps) = 1.2
where
T_clk: the new clock period, in picoseconds (ps)
max: the largest of the listed stage delays: IF, ID, the two EX halves, MEM and WB
G: the throughput gain over the 5-stage design, whose period was 300 ps
ps: picoseconds, 10^-12 seconds
In words: splitting EX removes the 300 ps stage, so the 250 ps IF and MEM stages now set a clock that is 1.2 times faster.
```

1. Next bottleneck: IF and MEM at 250 ps (the caches). Real designs split cache access across two or more stages for exactly this reason.
2. Cost: one more stage of register overhead and, as the next lessons show, potentially changed hazard penalties, depending on the affected paths.

lessons.title: Resource conflicts and register dependences
lessons.summary: Recognise structural hazards and distinguish true register data flow from register-name reuse.
lessons.body:
Use IF, ID, EX, MEM and WB from the preceding pipeline units. Keep the model assumptions below: the exact stall counts follow from the stated stage timing, not from the RISC-V instruction set itself.

This lesson uses a single-issue, in-order five-stage teaching pipeline with one-cycle stages, cache hits, register writes before reads in the same cycle, and the stated bypass paths. Numerical stalls below belong to this model, not every real CPU.

The earlier overlap unit's pipeline diagram assumed every instruction could start the cycle after the previous one. Real programs break that assumption constantly. The very next instruction often needs the result the current one is still computing.

A situation that prevents the next instruction from starting in its slot is a **hazard**. There are three kinds, and the hardware has a different trick for each. Whatever is left over shows up as extra CPI.

## Structural hazards

A **structural hazard** happens when two instructions need the same piece of hardware in the same cycle.

The classic example is memory. In cycle 4, instruction i1 is in MEM reading data while i4 is in IF fetching an instruction. With one single-ported memory, one of them must wait.

Possible fixes include stalling, adding ports or separating resources. Many CPUs use **separate L1 instruction and data caches** (a "modified Harvard" design), and register files often have multiple read and write ports. The ideal five-stage design assumes sufficient independent resources to avoid these structural hazards; in wider, real processors they appear as contention for ports and functional units.

## Data hazards

Consider:

```
add x1, x2, x3   # x1 = x2 + x3
sub x4, x1, x5   # needs the new x1
```

`sub` reads its registers in ID, in cycle 3. But `add` only writes x1 in WB, in cycle 5. If nothing intervenes, `sub` reads the *old* x1. This is a **read-after-write (RAW)** hazard, also called a true dependence.

```
cycle  1   2   3   4   5
add    IF  ID  EX  MEM WB
sub        IF  ID  ...

add writes x1 in cycle 5 (WB)
sub reads x1 in cycle 3 (ID): too early
```

### Option 1: stall

The simplest fix is for the hardware to detect the dependence in ID and hold `sub` there, inserting **bubbles** (do-nothing slots, effectively `nop`s) into EX until `add` has written x1.

A common trick helps: the register file is written in the first half of a cycle and read in the second half. So `sub` can read x1 in the same cycle that `add` writes it back (cycle 5). That still means `sub` waits in ID for cycles 3 and 4: **two stall cycles** for every back-to-back dependency. Since dependent instructions are extremely common, this would be ruinous for CPI.

### WAR and WAW

There are two other orderings of register access:

- **Write after read (WAR)**: a later instruction writes a register an earlier one still needs to read.
- **Write after write (WAW)**: two instructions write the same register, and the final value must come from the later one.

These are **name dependences**: they exist only because two instructions happen to reuse a register name, not because data flows between them. In the in-order 5-stage pipeline they cannot cause trouble, since every instruction reads in ID and writes in WB in program order. They become real problems in out-of-order processors, where **register renaming** removes them (the later register-renaming unit).

## Key takeaways
- A shared single memory port can conflict between instruction fetch and data access.
- RAW carries a produced value; WAR and WAW arise from reuse of register names.
- The stated register timing permits same-cycle write then read, leaving two stalls without bypasses.

## Further reading
- [MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining](https://computationstructures.org/notes/performance/notes.html)
- [RISC-V unprivileged ISA specification](https://riscv.github.io/riscv-isa-manual/snapshot/spec/)
- [BOOM implementation: rename stage](https://docs.boom-core.org/en/latest/sections/rename-stage.html)

questions.prompt: A simple pipelined CPU has a single-ported memory with at most one access per CPU cycle shared by instructions and data. In cycle 4, a load in MEM and a new instruction in IF both need it. What kind of hazard is this, and what is the usual fix?

options.text: A data hazard; fix it with forwarding
options.explanation: Data hazards are about one instruction needing another's result. Here the two instructions don't share any data; they want the same hardware.

options.text: A control hazard; fix it with branch prediction
options.explanation: Control hazards are about not knowing which instruction comes next. Nothing here involves a branch.

options.text: A structural hazard; fix it with separate instruction and data caches
options.explanation: Correct. Separate instruction/data caches are one way to remove this conflict; adding ports or stalling are alternatives. Not every modern CPU has the same cache structure.

options.text: Not a hazard; memory is fast enough to serve both
options.explanation: A single-ported memory can serve only one access per cycle, however fast it is.

questions.workedExample: Both instructions need the same limited port, giving a structural hazard. Separate access resources can remove it; alternatively stall one instruction or provide a suitable additional port.

questions.prompt:
Select every dependence that exists in this code.

```
# Labels mark program order.
i1: add x1, x2, x3
i2: sub x4, x1, x5
i3: mul x2, x6, x7
i4: add x4, x8, x9
```

options.text: i2 has a RAW (true) dependence on i1 through x1
options.explanation: Correct. i1 writes x1 and i2 reads it: data really flows from i1 to i2.

options.text: i3 has a RAW dependence on i2
options.explanation: Incorrect. i3 reads x6 and x7, neither of which i2 writes.

options.text: i3 has a WAR dependence on i1 through x2
options.explanation: Correct. i1 reads x2 and i3 later overwrites it. If i3 wrote first, i1 would read the wrong value. This is a name dependence.

options.text: i4 has a RAW dependence on i3
options.explanation: Incorrect. i4 reads x8 and x9; i3 writes x2.

options.text: i4 has a WAW dependence on i2 through x4
options.explanation: Correct. Both write x4, and the final value must be i4's. Another name dependence.

questions.workedExample:
List each instruction's reads and writes:

| | Writes | Reads |
|---|---|---|
| i1 | x1 | x2, x3 |
| i2 | x4 | x1, x5 |
| i3 | x2 | x6, x7 |
| i4 | x4 | x8, x9 |

1. Write then later read: x1 (i1 → i2) is **RAW**.
2. Read then later write: x2 (i1 → i3) is **WAR**.
3. Write then later write: x4 (i2 → i4) is **WAW**.
4. In an in-order 5-stage pipeline only the RAW needs handling; renaming in an out-of-order core removes the WAR and WAW.

lessons.title: Forward values and handle load-use stalls
lessons.summary: Choose the newest available result, exclude the zero register and explain the remaining one-cycle load-use gap.
lessons.body:
This unit uses the scalar five-stage pipeline with one-cycle cache-hit stages and operand bypasses into EX. A dependent instruction needs its input at the start of EX; an ALU result appears at the end of EX, while loaded data appears at the end of MEM.

> [!warning] Exclude the zero register
> RISC-V x0 always reads zero and discards writes. A forwarding comparison must reject destination x0: otherwise an attempted write could be incorrectly supplied to a later reader. For example, `add x0, x1, x2` must not affect the x0 operand of `add x3, x0, x4`.

### Option 2: forwarding

The key observation: the value `sub` needs exists at the end of `add`'s EX stage, in cycle 3. It just hasn't reached the register file yet. **Forwarding** (also called **bypassing**) adds wires and multiplexers that route results from the pipeline registers straight back to the ALU inputs.

```
         +-------------------+
         |  forward EX/MEM   |
         v                   |
ID/EX -> ALU -> EX/MEM -> MEM/WB
         ^                     |
         |  forward MEM/WB     |
         +---------------------+
```

There are two main paths:

- **EX/MEM to EX**: the result of the instruction directly ahead (one instruction back).
- **MEM/WB to EX**: the result of the instruction two ahead.

A **forwarding unit** compares the source register numbers of the instruction entering EX with the destination register numbers in EX/MEM and MEM/WB. If they match (and the earlier instruction really writes a register, and the register isn't x0), it selects the forwarded value instead of the stale one from ID/EX. If both match, the most recent producer takes priority, but its value must actually be available: a load in EX/MEM does not yet provide its loaded data. Stalling must prevent accidentally forwarding that load’s address or an older superseded value.

With forwarding, `add` followed by `sub` runs with **zero stalls**.

### The load-use hazard

Forwarding cannot fix everything. A load's data only arrives at the end of MEM:

```
lw  x1, 0(x2)    IF ID EX MEM WB
add x3, x1, x4      IF ID -- EX  MEM WB
                          ^ bubble
```

`add` needs x1 at the start of its EX. If `add` ran in cycle 4, it would need a value that `lw` only produces at the end of cycle 4. Time cannot run backwards, so the hardware must stall for **one cycle**, then forward from MEM/WB. This is the **load-use hazard**, and a **hazard detection unit** in ID spots it: "the instruction in EX is a load, and its destination is one of my sources".

## Key takeaways
- EX/MEM and MEM/WB bypasses can supply a result before register write-back.
- A newer producer wins, but an unavailable load result must stall rather than forward its address.
- A next-instruction EX consumer of a load needs one stall in this teaching model.

## Further reading
- [RISC-V unprivileged ISA specification](https://riscv.github.io/riscv-isa-manual/snapshot/spec/)
- [MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining](https://computationstructures.org/notes/performance/notes.html)

questions.prompt:
On the 5-stage pipeline **with full forwarding**, how many stall cycles does this pair need?

```
# The second instruction reads new x1.
add x1, x2, x3
sub x4, x1, x5
```

options.explanation: Correct. `add`'s result is at the end of its EX stage; it is forwarded from the EX/MEM register straight into the ALU for `sub`'s EX in the next cycle.
One stall is the load-use case. An ALU result is ready a cycle earlier than a load's, so no stall is needed.
Two stalls is what you get *without* forwarding, waiting for `add` to write back and `sub` to read in the same cycle.
Three stalls would only happen with no forwarding *and* a register file that cannot be written and read in the same cycle. With forwarding there are none.

questions.workedExample:
```
cycle  1  2  3  4   5
add    IF ID EX MEM WB
sub       IF ID EX  MEM
              ^ x1 from EX/MEM
```

1. `add` computes x1 during cycle 3 (EX).
2. `sub` needs x1 at the start of cycle 4 (its EX).
3. The forwarding path EX/MEM → ALU delivers it just in time.
4. Stalls: **0**.

questions.prompt:
With full forwarding, how many stall cycles does this pair need?

```
# The consumer needs the loaded x1.
lw  x1, 0(x2)
add x3, x1, x4
```

options.explanation: Forwarding can't help here: the loaded value doesn't exist until the end of MEM, which is after `add` would need it.
Two would be without forwarding. With forwarding, MEM/WB → EX delivers the value after just one bubble.
Correct. This is the load-use hazard: one bubble, then forward from MEM/WB into `add`'s EX.
A stall lasts only until the value is available, not until the load has fully left the pipeline.

questions.workedExample:
```
cycle  1  2  3  4   5   6
lw     IF ID EX MEM WB
add       IF ID --  EX  MEM
                    ^ x1 from MEM/WB
```

1. `lw` reads memory during cycle 4 (MEM); the value is ready at the end of cycle 4.
2. Without a stall, `add` would be in EX in cycle 4, needing it at the *start* of cycle 4. Impossible.
3. Insert one bubble; `add` executes in cycle 5 with x1 forwarded from MEM/WB.
4. Stalls: **1**.

questions.prompt:
With full forwarding, `and` enters EX. Which value of x1 does the forwarding unit supply?

```
add x1, x2, x3   # now in MEM/WB
sub x1, x1, x4   # now in EX/MEM
and x5, x1, x6   # entering EX
```

options.text: The value from the register file
options.explanation: The consumer needs the newest value from SUB. Even if the older ADD has updated the register file during this cycle, it is not the value required by program order.

options.text: The `add` result from MEM/WB
options.explanation: Both pipeline registers hold a new x1, but `add`'s is older. Using it would ignore `sub`'s update.

options.text: The `sub` result from EX/MEM
options.explanation: Correct. When both EX/MEM and MEM/WB match, the forwarding unit prefers the most recent result, from EX/MEM, matching program order.

options.text: It must stall; two matches are a conflict
options.explanation: No stall is needed. The priority rule (most recent wins) resolves it.

questions.workedExample:
1. Program order says `and` must see the x1 written by `sub`, the most recent writer.
2. `sub` is one instruction ahead, so its result is in EX/MEM.
3. `add` is two ahead; its x1 is in MEM/WB but has been superseded.
4. Textbook forwarding logic only uses MEM/WB if EX/MEM does **not** also match. So: EX/MEM wins.

questions.prompt:
A student's forwarding unit lacks the "destination ≠ x0" check. Before this code runs, the sum of registers x1 and x2 is 7, and register x4 holds 5. What ends up in x3, and what should?

```
# Writing x0 must discard the result.
add x0, x1, x2
add x3, x0, x4
```

options.text: x3 gets 12; it should get 5
options.explanation: Correct. The buggy unit sees that the first instruction's destination (x0) matches a source of the second and forwards 7 instead of using the hard-wired zero. Correct result: 0 + 5 = 5.

options.text: x3 gets 5 either way; writes to x0 are discarded
options.explanation: The register file does discard the write, but forwarding bypasses the register file. Without the check, the 7 is forwarded anyway.

options.text: x3 gets 7; it should get 12
options.explanation: Neither number is right. The second instruction adds x0 and x4, so the buggy value is 7 + 5 and the correct value is 0 + 5.

options.text: The pipeline stalls forever
options.explanation: The stated missing zero-register check selects a wrong forwarded value; it does not introduce a condition that stalls the pipeline forever.

questions.workedExample:
1. x0 always reads as 0 in RISC-V and MIPS; writes to it are ignored.
2. Instruction 1 computes 7 and holds 'destination = x0' in EX/MEM.
3. Instruction 2 has source x0. The buggy unit matches 0 == 0 and forwards 7.

```formula
x3 = x0 + x4
x3_bug = 7 + 5 = 12
x3_ok = 0 + 5 = 5
where
x3, x0, x4: RISC-V registers; the second instruction writes the sum of x0 and x4 into x3
x3_bug: the value x3 gets when the forwarding unit wrongly supplies the 7 computed for x0
x3_ok: the correct value, using the hard-wired zero in x0
In words: forwarding the discarded 7 gives 12, but x0 must always read as 0, so the right answer is 5.
```

Fix: forward only if the earlier instruction writes a register **and** its destination is not x0.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the load-use hazard in the 5-stage pipeline are true?

options.text: Forwarding alone can't remove it, because the loaded value only exists at the end of MEM
options.explanation: True. The consumer's EX would coincide with the load's MEM, so the data arrives too late however you route it.

options.text: It is detected in ID, by checking whether the instruction in EX is a load whose destination matches a source
options.explanation: True for an EX-stage consumer in this model, excluding writes to zero and operands not actually read. A store-data operand with a later bypass can need different handling.

options.text: The stall is created by freezing the PC and IF/ID register and inserting a bubble into ID/EX
options.explanation: True. Holding PC and IF/ID repeats the fetch and decode; zeroing the control signals in ID/EX makes EX do nothing for a cycle.

options.text: A load followed by a store of the loaded register can never avoid the stall, even with forwarding into MEM
options.explanation: False. The store needs the value only as data to write in MEM, so a MEM/WB → MEM forwarding path can avoid the stall. Whether a given design has that path varies.

options.text: Out-of-order cores eliminate load latency
options.explanation: False. They *hide* it by running independent instructions while the load is in flight. The latency is still there and shows up when there is no independent work.

questions.workedExample:
1. Timing: `lw` data ready at end of cycle 4; next instruction's EX would be cycle 4. Too late, so a stall is required for ALU consumers.
2. Detection: in ID, compare the source registers with ID/EX's destination when ID/EX holds a load.
3. Mechanism: hold PC and IF/ID (fetch and decode repeat), clear ID/EX control bits (a bubble).
4. Stores of loaded data need the value later (MEM, not EX), so extra forwarding can avoid it.
5. Out-of-order execution overlaps latency; it can't make a cache access take zero time.

lessons.title: Schedule independent work around a load
lessons.summary: Reorder a straight-line sequence without changing its values or observable memory behaviour.
lessons.body:
Continue with a five-stage, single-issue, cache-hit teaching pipeline. ALU-to-ALU forwarding needs no stall; a load immediately followed by an EX consumer needs one. Scheduling fills that gap with useful independent work rather than changing the hardware. The two listings below compute the same two independent expressions only under their stated memory assumptions.

### Option 3: let the compiler schedule around it

Since the load-use stall is predictable, the compiler can reorder independent instructions to fill the gap. For ordinary valid, nonvolatile memory accesses with independent values and no aliasing or observable-order constraints, take `a = b + c; d = e + f`. The listings below are schematic (symbolic addresses rather than literal RISC-V load/store syntax; `!` marks a load-use stall and is not an instruction):

```
# naive order        # scheduled
lw  x1, b            lw  x1, b
lw  x2, c            lw  x2, c
add x3, x1, x2  !    lw  x4, e
sw  x3, a            add x3, x1, x2
lw  x4, e            lw  x5, f
lw  x5, f            sw  x3, a
add x6, x4, x5  !    add x6, x4, x5
sw  x6, d            sw  x6, d
```

The naive order has two load-use stalls (marked `!`). In the scheduled order every load has an independent instruction between it and its first dependent operation, so there are none. Counting cycles for the 8 instructions from first fetch to last write-back:

```formula
N_cyc = k + (n − 1) + s_tot
N_naive = 5 + (8 − 1) + 2 = 14
N_sched = 5 + (8 − 1) + 0 = 12
where
N_cyc: the total clock cycles from the first fetch to the last write-back
k: the number of pipeline stages, 5
n: the number of instructions, 8 in each listing
s_tot: the total stall cycles (bubbles) in the run: 2 for the naive order, 0 for the scheduled one
N_naive, N_sched: the cycle counts for the naive and the scheduled order
In words: each stall adds one cycle to the ideal fill-plus-one-per-instruction count, so removing both stalls saves 2 of 14 cycles.
```

Compilers do this routinely (**instruction scheduling**), and it matters most on simple in-order cores when the target implements the assumed instruction timing.

## Key takeaways
- Move only independent operations across the load-use gap.
- Memory faults, aliasing, volatile accesses and observable order can forbid a reorder.
- Count one additional cycle for each remaining bubble in this finite-run model.

## Further reading
- [MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining](https://computationstructures.org/notes/performance/notes.html)
- [RISC-V unprivileged ISA specification](https://riscv.github.io/riscv-isa-manual/snapshot/spec/)

questions.prompt:
With forwarding, this code has two load-use stalls. Which reordering removes both while computing the same results?

```
# Each load immediately feeds an add.
lw  x1, 0(x10)
add x2, x1, x3
lw  x4, 4(x10)
add x5, x4, x6
```

Assume valid ordinary memory, no faults or observable volatile/I/O ordering, and the specified one-cycle stages.

options.text: `add x5` first, then the rest in order
options.explanation: Wrong: `add x5` would read x4 before it has been loaded, giving a different result.

options.text: Swap the two `add`s
options.explanation: Then `add x5` comes before `lw x4`, which reads x4 before it is loaded and changes the result.

options.text: Insert a `nop` after each load
options.explanation: This avoids the hardware stall but takes exactly as many cycles; the bubble just becomes an explicit instruction.

options.text: `lw x1`, `lw x4`, `add x2`, `add x5`
options.explanation: Correct. Each load is now two instructions ahead of its use, so MEM/WB forwarding delivers in time. No stalls, and no dependence is violated since the two halves are independent.

questions.workedExample:
1. The two pairs (`lw x1`/`add x2`, `lw x4`/`add x5`) are independent: they touch different registers.
2. Hoisting `lw x4` above `add x2` is legal: `add x2` neither reads nor writes x4, and `lw x4` doesn't touch x1, x2 or x3.
3. New distances: `lw x1` → `add x2` is 2; `lw x4` → `add x5` is 2.
4. Both are covered by MEM/WB → EX forwarding: **0 stalls**, 8 cycles instead of 10.

lessons.title: Trace stalls with a dependency model
lessons.summary: Use a small readiness-slot simulation and recognise the hardware behaviour it intentionally omits.
lessons.body:
The previous unit compared two schedules for eight instructions. This unit turns the same assumptions into a small executable model: in-order issue, one-cycle stages, and all operands needed by EX. With forwarding, the earlier naive schedule had two stalls and its reordered version had none; without forwarding, same-cycle WB then ID determines when a consumer may continue.

### Counting stalls in code

This function counts stall cycles for a straight-line program on the 5-stage pipeline. It records the earliest logical issue slot compatible with each dependency. With forwarding this is not the cycle when the register file itself contains the new value. Program entries are `(op, dst, srcs)` with integer register IDs 0–31, `dst=None` for no register result, and register 0 hard-wired to zero. All forwarded sources, including store data, are required by EX in this simplified model; it does not model a separate late store-data bypass, branches, cache misses or multicycle units:

```python
def stalls(prog, forwarding=True):
    rdy = {}     # reg -> ready slot
    cycle = 0    # logical issue slot
    total = 0
    for op, dst, srcs in prog:
        need = [rdy.get(r, 0)
                for r in srcs if r != 0]
        # Wait for operands and issue turn.
        start = max(need + [cycle])
        total += start - cycle
        cycle = start
        # Register zero never gains a value.
        if dst:
            if not forwarding:
                lat = 3      # wait for WB
            elif op == "lw":
                lat = 2      # load-use
            else:
                lat = 1      # EX -> EX
            # Track the newest version.
            rdy[dst] = cycle + lat
        cycle += 1
    # Return extra issue slots.
    return total
```

On the naive sequence above it returns 2 with forwarding and 8 without; on the scheduled one, 0 and 4. For this sequence and model, forwarding removes more stalls than scheduling alone; combining them removes all modelled stalls.

## Key takeaways
- Readiness slots represent when a dependent operation may start, not register-file update time.
- Loads and ordinary ALU results have different forwarding latencies.
- This model omits branches, cache misses, multicycle units and a late store-data bypass.

## Further reading
- [MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining](https://computationstructures.org/notes/performance/notes.html)
- [RISC-V unprivileged ISA specification](https://riscv.github.io/riscv-isa-manual/snapshot/spec/)

On the 5-stage pipeline with full forwarding, how many cycles does this sequence take from the first IF to the last WB?

```

lw  x1, 0(x2)
add x3, x1, x4
sub x5, x3, x1
or  x6, x5, x7
```

options.explanation: 8 is the no-hazard count (5 + 3). It misses the load-use stall between `lw` and `add`.
Correct. 4 instructions take 5 + 3 = 8 cycles ideally. The `lw` → `add` pair adds 1 stall. The other dependences are ALU → ALU, covered by forwarding. Total 9.
This adds a stall for every dependence. Only the load-use one stalls when forwarding is available.
14 is the count *without* forwarding: 3 dependent pairs × 2 stalls = 6 stalls, plus 8.

questions.workedExample:
Check each dependence:

```
lw  -> add  (x1)  load-use: 1 stall
add -> sub  (x3)  ALU->ALU: 0
lw  -> sub  (x1)  2+ apart: 0
sub -> or   (x5)  ALU->ALU: 0
```

Then add the stalls to the ideal pipelined cycle count:

```formula
N_cyc = k + (n − 1) + s_tot
N_cyc = 5 + 3 + 1 = 9
N_nofwd = 5 + 3 + 6 = 14
where
N_cyc: the cycles from the first IF to the last WB, with forwarding
k: the number of pipeline stages, 5
n: the number of instructions, 4
s_tot: the total stall cycles: 1 with forwarding (the load-use pair)
N_nofwd: the cycle count without forwarding, where each of the 3 back-to-back dependences costs 2 stalls (6 in all)
In words: 8 cycles for four instructions plus one load-use bubble makes 9; without forwarding, six bubbles make 14.
```

lessons.title: Control hazards and additive CPI
lessons.summary: Compare branch-resolution choices and combine nonoverlapping hazard penalties.
lessons.body:
Use the same scalar IF–ID–EX–MEM–WB teaching design. The earlier data-hazard units established forwarding and one-cycle load-use stalls; this unit adds branch control flow. All branch penalties below specify their resolution stage and prediction rule, so they are model-specific.

## Control hazards

After fetching a branch in cycle 1, what should IF fetch in cycle 2? The branch hasn't even been decoded, let alone compared its registers. This is a **control hazard**.

Suppose the branch outcome is known at the end of EX (cycle 3). Options:

1. **Stall** until the branch resolves: 2 lost cycles on every branch.
2. **Predict not taken**: keep fetching sequentially. If the branch isn't taken, no cost. If it is, **flush** the two wrongly fetched instructions (turn them into bubbles) and fetch from the target: a 2-cycle penalty.
3. **Resolve earlier**: add a comparator and target adder in ID so the branch is decided in cycle 2. The penalty falls to 1 cycle, but now the branch may need forwarding into ID and can stall on an instruction ahead of it.
4. **Branch delay slot**: classic MIPS normal delay slots execute on both paths; some branch-likely forms have annulment rules. The compiler fills the slot with useful work when it can (or a `nop`). It provides one architecturally executed slot; that does not necessarily hide the entire branch penalty of a particular implementation, but became a burden when pipelines got deeper and wider. RISC-V and ARM64 do not have delay slots.

Real processors use **dynamic branch prediction**, covered in the following prediction units.

## Putting numbers on it

For a long run in this scalar model, ignoring fill/drain and avoiding double-counting overlapping penalties, hazards add stall cycles to the ideal CPI of 1. Each hazard type contributes how often it can occur, times how often it actually bites, times what it costs:

```formula
CPI = 1 + s
s = Σ_h (F_h × p_h × c_h)
where
CPI: cycles per instruction, the average clock cycles per completed instruction
1: the ideal CPI of a single-issue pipeline, which completes one instruction per cycle when nothing stalls
s: the average stall cycles per instruction
Σ_h: sigma: add up the bracketed term over every hazard type h
h: one hazard type, such as load-use stalls or taken branches
F_h: the fraction of all instructions that can cause hazard h (for example, the fraction that are loads), between 0 and 1
p_h: the probability that such an instruction actually causes the stall (for example, that the next instruction depends on the load), between 0 and 1
c_h: the penalty each time, in stall cycles
In words: CPI is one plus the average number of stall cycles per instruction, and each hazard adds its frequency times its probability times its penalty.
```

A worked example: 25% of instructions are loads, and 40% of those are immediately followed by a dependent instruction (1-cycle stall each). 15% are branches; with predict-not-taken, 60% of them are taken, costing 2 cycles. Assume these penalties are additive, and the stated dependencies need operands in EX:

```formula
s_load = 0.25 × 0.4 × 1 = 0.10
s_br = 0.15 × 0.6 × 2 = 0.18
CPI = 1 + s_load + s_br
CPI = 1 + 0.10 + 0.18 = 1.28
where
s_load: the stall cycles per instruction from load-use hazards: fraction of loads × fraction followed by a dependent instruction × 1-cycle penalty
s_br: the stall cycles per instruction from taken branches: fraction of branches × fraction taken × 2-cycle penalty
CPI: cycles per instruction including the stalls
In words: load-use stalls add 0.10 cycles and taken branches add 0.18 cycles to every instruction on average, so CPI rises from 1 to 1.28.
```

Notice branches cost more than loads here. That is why branch prediction gets an entire lesson, and why it matters even more in deeper pipelines, where recovery penalties may be larger. Exact real-core cycle counts require a specified core and measurement.

> [!note] Keep the earlier zero-register rule
> The data-hazard units also excluded writes to RISC-V x0 from forwarding. Control-hazard accounting does not relax that correctness requirement.

## Key takeaways
- Resolving a branch later leaves more sequential fetches to discard in the stated model.
- Earlier resolution can trade fewer flushes for operand waits or a slower clock.
- Add hazard contributions only when their costs do not overlap.

## Further reading
- [MIPS architecture manual: branches and delay slots](https://hades.mech.northwestern.edu/images/a/af/MIPS32_Architecture_Volume_I-A_Introduction.pdf)
- [RISC-V unprivileged ISA specification](https://riscv.github.io/riscv-isa-manual/snapshot/spec/)
- [BOOM implementation: branch prediction](https://docs.boom-core.org/en/latest/sections/branch-prediction/index.html)

questions.prompt: In a program, 30% of instructions are loads and half of them are immediately followed by a dependent instruction. 20% are branches; the pipeline resolves branches in ID with a 1-cycle penalty when taken, and 50% are taken. With full forwarding and no other stalls, what is the CPI? Assume every stated load-use dependency needs its operand in EX, no additional branch operand stalls, additive penalties and negligible fill/drain.

options.explanation: Correct. Load-use stalls add 0.3 × 0.5 × 1 = 0.15 cycles per instruction and branches add 0.2 × 0.5 × 1 = 0.10, so CPI is 1 + 0.15 + 0.10 = 1.25.
This charges every load and every branch a stall (0.3 + 0.2). Only loads followed by a dependent instruction, and taken branches, stall.
This counts the load stalls but forgets the branch penalty.
This uses a 2-cycle branch penalty (as if resolved in EX). The question says branches resolve in ID with a 1-cycle penalty.

questions.workedExample:
For each hazard: fraction of instructions × probability it bites × penalty.

```formula
s_ld = 0.30 × 0.5 × 1 = 0.15
s_br = 0.20 × 0.5 × 1 = 0.10
CPI = 1 + s_ld + s_br
CPI = 1 + 0.15 + 0.10 = 1.25
where
s_ld: the load-use stall cycles per instruction: 30% are loads, half of those have an immediate dependent, 1 stall each
s_br: the branch stall cycles per instruction: 20% are branches, half are taken, 1 cycle each
CPI: cycles per instruction; 1 is the ideal for this pipeline with no stalls
In words: the stalls add a quarter of a cycle to every instruction on average, so CPI is 1.25.
```

questions.prompt: 20% of instructions are branches and 60% of branches are taken. Design A resolves branches in EX (2-cycle taken penalty, predict not-taken). Design B resolves in ID (1-cycle taken penalty), but 30% of branches then stall 1 cycle waiting for an operand from the previous ALU instruction, and the extra comparator lengthens the clock by 3%. Assume these stall and taken-branch costs add without overlap; otherwise CPI is 1. Which is faster?

options.text: A, because B has a slower clock
options.explanation: B’s period is 3% longer (its frequency is divided by 1.03), but the CPI reduction more than compensates in the stated model.

options.text: B, by about 5%, from its lower CPI
options.explanation: This compares CPI only (1.24 vs 1.18) and forgets B's 3% longer clock.

options.text: They are identical
options.explanation: Time per instruction is 1.24 for A and about 1.215 for B (in A's clock units). Close, but not equal.

options.text: B, by about 2%
options.explanation: Correct. A has CPI 1.24. B has CPI 1.18 but each cycle takes 3% longer. B’s resulting time per instruction is about 1.215 original cycles, making B about 1.02 times faster.

questions.workedExample:
Time per instruction is CPI times the clock period. Take A's clock period as 1.

```formula
t = CPI × T_clk
CPI_A = 1 + 0.2 × 0.6 × 2 = 1.24
CPI_B = 1 + 0.2 × 0.6 × 1 + 0.2 × 0.3
CPI_B = 1.18
t_A = 1.24 × 1 = 1.24
t_B = 1.18 × 1.03 ≈ 1.215
S = t_A / t_B = 1.24 / 1.215 ≈ 1.02
where
t, t_A, t_B: the average time per instruction, in units of A's clock period
CPI, CPI_A, CPI_B: cycles per instruction; 1 is the ideal
T_clk: the clock period: 1 for A, 1.03 for B (3% longer)
0.2 × 0.6: branches (20%) that are taken (60%); they cost 2 cycles on A and 1 on B
0.2 × 0.3: branches (20%) that stall 1 cycle on B waiting for an operand (30% of them)
S: the speedup of B over A
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: B saves 0.06 cycles per instruction but its clock is 3% slower, leaving it only about 2% faster.
```

Real design decisions often come down to margins this thin, which is why architects simulate rather than guess.

lessons.title: Cost branch misses and apply static rules
lessons.summary: Estimate additive branch CPI and distinguish fixed prediction rules from learned behaviour.
lessons.body:
A processor can fetch and execute instructions beyond a branch before its direction and target are known. If its prediction is wrong, it must discard younger wrong-path work and redirect execution. How much work is lost depends on the processor and when the branch resolves.

> [!note] Evidence limits
> Universal branch frequencies, prediction accuracies, pipeline depths and product-specific predictor details are omitted: they need a named workload and reliable documentation or measurements. The numerical examples below are explicit teaching models.

## What a misprediction costs

In an additive model with a fixed average recovery penalty and no overlap with other counted stalls, mispredictions add this many cycles to every instruction on average:

```formula
CPI_br = F_br × m × c_mis
m = 1 − A
where
CPI_br: the extra cycles per instruction caused by branch mispredictions
F_br: the branch fraction: the share of executed instructions that are branches, between 0 and 1
m: the misprediction rate: the share of branches predicted wrongly, between 0 and 1
A: the predictor's accuracy: the share of branches predicted correctly, between 0 and 1
c_mis: the misprediction penalty: the cycles lost recovering from each wrong prediction
In words: only mispredicted branches cost anything, so the extra CPI is how often branches occur, times how often they are guessed wrong, times what each wrong guess costs.
```

### Why 95% isn't good enough

Assume unchanged retired instruction count and clock frequency, with additive penalties. 20% of instructions are branches, the predictor is 95% accurate, and the penalty is 15 cycles. The core is 4-wide, with an ideal CPI of 0.25 when every prediction is right:

```formula
CPI_br = 0.2 × (1 − 0.95) × 15 = 0.15
CPI = CPI_base + CPI_br
CPI = 0.25 + 0.15 = 0.40
S = CPI / CPI_base = 0.40 / 0.25 = 1.6
where
CPI_br: the extra cycles per instruction from mispredictions
CPI_base: the CPI with perfect prediction, 0.25 for this 4-wide core (it can finish up to 4 instructions per cycle)
CPI: the actual average cycles per instruction
S: the slowdown factor relative to perfect prediction; with the same instruction count and clock, time is proportional to CPI
In words: 5% of branches being wrong adds 0.15 cycles to every instruction, which makes this core 1.6 times slower than with perfect prediction.
```

The program runs **1.6× slower** than with perfect prediction. Getting to 98% accuracy, with the other assumptions unchanged, brings the extra branch contribution down to 0.06 cycles per instruction. The wrong-prediction fraction is now 2% rather than 5%.

Lower base CPI makes a given additional CPI more significant. Width and pipeline organisation can affect recovery, but neither alone determines a universal penalty or area cost.

## Static prediction

The simplest predictors use fixed rules with no history:

- **Always not taken**: just keep fetching sequentially. Simple; it misses each taken iteration of a loop-back branch.
- **Backward taken, forward not taken (BTFN)**: a branch that jumps backwards is probably a loop, so predict taken; a forward branch is probably an `if`, so predict not taken. This is a heuristic, not a guarantee about source-level control flow.

Compilers help by laying out code so the likely path falls through. GCC and Clang's `__builtin_expect`, C++20's `[[likely]]` and `[[unlikely]]`, and profile-guided optimisation can inform these layout and optimisation decisions; they do not guarantee a particular hardware predictor action.

## Key takeaways
- Branch fraction, miss rate and recovery cycles determine the additive miss contribution.
- A small additional CPI is a larger slowdown when base CPI is already low.
- BTFN is a direction heuristic; compiler hints guide optimisation without guaranteeing hardware action.

## Further reading
- [McFarling: Combining Branch Predictors (original report)](https://shiftleft.com/mirrors/www.hpl.hp.com/techreports/Compaq-DEC/WRL-TN-36.pdf)
- [GCC: branch expectation built-in](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Other-Builtins.html)
- [BOOM implementation: branch prediction](https://docs.boom-core.org/en/latest/sections/branch-prediction/index.html)

questions.prompt: 25% of a program's instructions are branches, the predictor is 90% accurate, and each misprediction costs 12 cycles. How much CPI do mispredictions add? Use the additive model, with no overlapping penalties.

options.explanation: Correct. 0.25 × 0.10 × 12 = 0.3 cycles per instruction.
This is branch fraction × penalty (0.25 × 12), as if every branch mispredicted. Only the 10% of branches that are mispredicted pay the penalty.
This uses the accuracy (90%) rather than the misprediction rate (10%). A correct prediction incurs no misprediction-recovery penalty in this model; prediction itself still uses resources.
This is misprediction rate × penalty (0.1 × 12), the extra cycles per *branch*, not per instruction.

questions.workedExample:
Only mispredicted branches pay the penalty:

```formula
CPI_br = F_br × (1 − A) × c_mis
CPI_br = 0.25 × (1 − 0.90) × 12
CPI_br = 0.25 × 0.10 × 12 = 0.3
where
CPI_br: the extra cycles per instruction from mispredictions
F_br: the fraction of instructions that are branches, 0.25
A: the predictor's accuracy, 0.90, so 1 − A = 0.10 is the misprediction rate
c_mis: the misprediction penalty, 12 cycles
In words: a quarter of instructions are branches, a tenth of those are guessed wrong, and each wrong guess costs 12 cycles, adding 0.3 cycles per instruction.
```

If the base CPI were 1, the program would run at CPI 1.3, so the recovery term would account for 0.3 / 1.3 ≈ 23% of modelled execution time.

questions.prompt: A static *backward taken, forward not taken* (BTFN) predictor sees a conditional branch at the bottom of a `for` loop that jumps back to the loop's start. What does it predict, and why?

options.text: Not taken, because static predictors always predict not taken
options.explanation: That is the simpler 'always not taken' rule. BTFN looks at the branch direction.

options.text: Taken, because backward branches are usually loops that repeat
options.explanation: Correct. Its target is backward, so the BTFN rule predicts taken. Repeated loop-back branches motivate this heuristic; not every backward branch is taken or belongs to a long loop.

options.text: It depends on the branch's previous outcome
options.explanation: Using previous outcomes is dynamic prediction. BTFN is static: it uses only the direction of the jump.

options.text: Taken, because forward branches are usually taken
options.explanation: BTFN predicts forward branches not taken. Source-level if/error-path layout depends on compilation and does not define the rule.

questions.workedExample: For the stated backward branch BTFN predicts taken without using execution history. If its outcomes are 99 taken followed by one not-taken exit, it is correct in 99 of every 100 outcomes.

questions.prompt: A 4-wide core has a base CPI of 0.3 with perfect prediction. 20% of instructions are branches and the misprediction penalty is 16 cycles. A new predictor improves accuracy from 94% to 97%. What speedup does that give? Assume unchanged retired instruction count and clock frequency, and additive nonoverlapping penalties.

options.text: About 1.03×, the same as the accuracy gain
options.explanation: The misprediction rate halves (6% to 3%), but the effect on total time depends on both the base CPI and the recovery term.

options.text: 2×, because the misprediction rate halved
options.explanation: Only the misprediction part of CPI halves; the base 0.3 does not change.

options.text: About 1.24×
About 1.5×
options.explanation: Overestimates: the 0.096 saved is about a fifth of the original CPI of 0.492, not a third.

questions.workedExample:
Add the misprediction term to the base CPI for each predictor:

```formula
CPI = CPI_0 + F_br × m × c_mis
CPI_old = 0.3 + 0.2 × 0.06 × 16 = 0.492
CPI_new = 0.3 + 0.2 × 0.03 × 16 = 0.396
S = 0.492 / 0.396 ≈ 1.24
where
CPI, CPI_old, CPI_new: cycles per instruction (with the old or new predictor)
CPI_0: the base CPI with perfect prediction, 0.3
F_br: the fraction of instructions that are branches, 0.2
m: the misprediction rate: 0.06 at 94% accuracy, 0.03 at 97%
c_mis: the misprediction penalty, 16 cycles
S: the speedup; with unchanged instruction count and clock, time is proportional to CPI
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: halving the misprediction rate halves only the recovery part of CPI, 0.192 down to 0.096, giving about 1.24 times the speed.
```

Recovery CPI halves; base CPI does not.
